title: Duplicate Handling
description: Choose SQL duplicate policies deliberately with DISTINCT, UNION and UNION ALL, preserving fact identity, provenance, null behavior and meaningful event multiplicity.
notes:
## Decide whether repetition represents information

Duplicate handling in SQL begins with a domain question: when do two result rows represent the same intended fact? Two ticket purchases can have the same price and still be separate purchases. Two imports can repeat the same external purchase identity and represent an accidental duplicate. Comparing visible values without stating the identity can erase legitimate events or retain a repeated event that should have been rejected.

SQL query results usually behave as bags, meaning repeated rows can survive. Set operations and DISTINCT introduce explicit duplicate policies. Read [UNION ALL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-all) and [UNION](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-sql) before comparing their results. This topic focuses on choosing and verifying the policy, rather than treating every repeated display row as an error.

## Separate duplicate rows from duplicate labels

Suppose two workshops have different workshop_id values but both use the title Introduction to SQL. Selecting workshop_id and title returns two different rows. Selecting only title can display the same string twice. Those repeated labels do not establish that the underlying workshop records are duplicates. The projection removed the identity that distinguished them.

A report of distinct workshop titles may legitimately merge the labels. A registration picker must usually retain the workshop identities so that a learner can select the intended event. Both queries can read the same table and both can be correct, because they serve different output contracts. Define the caller's required identity before applying DISTINCT or replacing a bag-preserving operation with a set operation.

## Understand the scope of DISTINCT

SELECT DISTINCT applies to the complete selected tuple. If a query selects learner_id and course_code, two rows collapse only when both selected values compare as duplicates under the applicable rules. DISTINCT is not an instruction to keep one arbitrary row per learner. Including a varying timestamp or row identity can prevent otherwise repeated visible attributes from collapsing.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT learner_id, course_code
FROM attendance_uploads
ORDER BY learner_id, course_code;
```

This query returns the represented learner-course pairs. It does not choose the latest attendance event, sum attendance duration or validate that repeated uploads were accidental. Those tasks require additional definitions. If the business rule concerns the newest event per learner and course, specify the ordering and tie policy, then use a suitable ranking or selection query.

## Compare UNION with UNION ALL precisely

UNION combines compatible query outputs and removes duplicate result tuples by default. UNION ALL combines them while retaining multiplicity. Duplicate removal applies across the combined result, including repeats originating within an individual branch. It is not restricted to a row appearing once on the left and once on the right.

```sql
SELECT learner_id, course_code FROM morning_uploads
UNION
SELECT learner_id, course_code FROM afternoon_uploads;
```

If the same learner-course pair appears three times in the morning and twice in the afternoon, UNION returns one copy of that projected pair. UNION ALL returns five copies. Whether one or five is correct depends on whether the rows represent membership pairs or separate events. A faster operation that changes that policy answers a different question.

## Keep provenance when sources matter

Adding a source label to each branch changes the tuple being compared. The pair learner seven with SQL from morning differs from learner seven with SQL from afternoon when source_name is selected. UNION therefore retains both tuples even if the learner and course values agree. This can be useful for tracing where records came from, but it is not equivalent to distinct membership across sources.

If the report needs both a unified membership list and provenance, model those as related outputs rather than assuming one projection satisfies both. You might aggregate source labels separately or preserve raw events in a staging relation while deriving the distinct membership view. Do not discard source evidence prematurely when corrections, reconciliation or auditability depend on knowing which input supplied each observation.

## Know the relevant null rule

Duplicate elimination treats nulls as not distinct for the relevant set comparison. Two selected tuples with the same other values and null in the same selected position can collapse into one tuple under DISTINCT or UNION. That behavior differs from ordinary equality predicates, where NULL equals NULL does not evaluate true.

A missing course_code in two uploads therefore does not automatically represent two different set values. It also does not prove the two uploads refer to the same real-world course. Set duplicate policy is an operation on the projected values. If missing identity makes reliable deduplication impossible, preserve uncertainty instead of interpreting the set result as proof that one underlying event occurred.

## Compare text under actual collation rules

Text duplicate comparison can depend on the output's collation. Labels differing in letter case may compare equal under a case-insensitive collation. This means a visually distinct spelling is not guaranteed to survive duplicate elimination as a separate value. Conversely, two labels that look similar can differ in meaningful characters that the chosen comparison retains.

Choose comparison semantics from the domain rather than from whichever collation a temporary table inherits. A case-insensitive person-name search and a case-sensitive external token have different requirements. When combining branches, inspect compatible types and collations as part of the result contract. Do not assume that adding DISTINCT creates a universal byte-for-byte deduplication procedure for every kind of text.

## Diagnose repetition created by joins

A learner joined to three attendance rows appears three times in the pair-level result. Selecting only learner detail can make those three outputs look like accidental duplicates. If the requirement is learners with any attendance, an EXISTS membership query often states the intended grain more clearly. If the requirement is every attendance event, removing the repeated learner detail loses information about event multiplicity.

A final DISTINCT can hide an incomplete join predicate because some incorrect pairs happen to project identical columns. Before using it as a repair, inspect relationship keys and expected cardinality. Count source identities where needed and include distinct entities with equal labels in the fixture. Correct duplicate handling should preserve the requested facts, not simply make the result look less repetitive.

## Distinguish result cleanup from integrity enforcement

SELECT DISTINCT changes a query result; it does not remove rows from storage or prevent future duplicate imports. A unique constraint or unique index can enforce an approved key invariant at write time. Such schema changes require separate review and authorization in a real application. Do not present a read-time deduplication query as equivalent protection against concurrent duplicate writes.

Similarly, deleting repeated stored records requires a survivor policy, reference analysis and explicit operational approval. Keeping the smallest identity may discard the newest correction or break relationships if performed carelessly. The exercises here only read synthetic data. They teach how result policies behave without claiming to solve production cleanup, identity resolution or data-retention requirements.

## Use multiplicity deliberately in measures

COUNT(*) after UNION ALL counts retained observations, while COUNT(*) after a distinct union counts distinct projected tuples. Neither is inherently the right count of people or events. The projection and duplicate policy determine the population being counted. State that population in the output label so that a reader does not mistake upload observations for unique enrollments.

The same reasoning applies to sums. Removing duplicate numeric amounts can undercount legitimate equal-valued transactions. Preserving repeated imported events can overcount accidental replays. Deduplicate by a verified event identity when the contract supports it, and keep separate legitimate events even when all displayed measures happen to agree. A fixture with two distinct five-unit transactions is more revealing than one where every amount is different.

## Verify overlap, repetition and absence independently

Build a tiny pair of sources with one tuple unique to each, one tuple shared across both, a repeat within one branch and a null-valued tuple. Predict the result multiplicities for UNION and UNION ALL before executing them. Then add an identity or source column and predict the changed comparison tuple. These cases separate cross-source overlap from within-source repetition and projection effects.

The exercises compare distinct membership with observation multiplicity using integer identities, avoiding accidental collation assumptions. Continue with [set compatibility](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/set-compatibility) for output alignment and [join cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality) for repetition caused by relationships. A clear duplicate policy names the compared tuple, the intended fact identity, the treatment of missing values and whether repetition is meaningful evidence.

questions.question_text: What is the default duplicate-handling behavior of UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT?
options: All three keep every duplicate by default
All three remove duplicates by default (set semantics)
UNION keeps duplicates, but INTERSECT and EXCEPT remove them
Duplicate handling is undefined and varies randomly
questions.explanation: Every one of these three operations deduplicates by default.

questions.question_text: Which MySQL 8.4 operation concatenates both inputs while retaining their combined copies?
options: INTERSECT ALL
EXCEPT ALL
UNION ALL
UNION DISTINCT
questions.explanation: UNION ALL adds the multiplicities from both branches without distinct elimination.

questions.question_text: For one tuple appearing m times on the left and n times on the right, how do MySQL 8.4 INTERSECT ALL and EXCEPT ALL differ?
options: Both always return m+n copies
INTERSECT ALL returns min(m,n); EXCEPT ALL returns max(m-n,0)
Both return exactly one copy
Neither syntax is supported in MySQL 8.4
questions.explanation: ALL preserves multiset semantics according to the operation; it is not synonymous with concatenation for every set operator.

questions.question_text: Do you ever need to explicitly opt OUT of deduplication to get the default deduplicating behavior?
options: Yes, deduplication must always be explicitly requested
No — deduplication IS the default; you explicitly opt INTO keeping duplicates instead (e.g. via ALL)
Deduplication cannot be controlled at all
This varies unpredictably by query
questions.explanation: Plain set forms eliminate duplicate tuples. ALL selects multiset rules: UNION ALL adds copies, INTERSECT ALL keeps the minimum count, and EXCEPT ALL subtracts counts without going below zero.

questions.question_text: Why does duplicate handling matter for a downstream COUNT(*) on a combined result?
options: COUNT(*) is unaffected by whether duplicates were removed
Whether duplicates were removed directly changes how many rows COUNT(*) sees
COUNT(*) automatically ignores duplicates regardless of the set operation used
This only matters for INTERSECT, never UNION
questions.explanation: The actual row count of the combined result depends directly on whether deduplication happened.

questions.question_text: What practical question should precede choosing between a plain set operation and its ALL variant?
options: Whether the tables have the same name
Whether duplicates actually need to be removed for this specific use case
Whether ORDER BY will be used
Whether the query involves more than one table
questions.explanation: This is the core cost/correctness trade-off to consider before defaulting to the deduplicating form.

questions.question_text: What is a careful performance statement about duplicate elimination?
options: It never costs work
It can require comparison or other processing, though a provably redundant step may be optimized away
It only matters for INTERSECT
Every plan must use the same sorting method
questions.explanation: Physical work depends on the selected plan and proven properties. Do not assert a mandatory algorithm or unavoidable cost when redundancy is provable.

questions.question_text: When do UNION and UNION ALL return the same bag of selected tuples from two branches?
options: Whenever there is no cross-branch overlap, even if a branch repeats tuples
When each branch has unique selected tuples and their tuple sets are disjoint
Whenever both branches have the same row count
Whenever ORDER BY is omitted
questions.explanation: Both within-branch uniqueness and cross-branch disjointness are required. Equal results do not by themselves establish a universal performance difference.

questions.question_text: What does SELECT DISTINCT compare?
options: The entire selected tuple
Only the first column
Only the primary key even if absent
Only numeric values
questions.explanation: All selected expressions define result equality.

questions.question_text: Does DISTINCT modify stored rows?
options: Yes, it deletes copies
No
Yes, it creates a unique index
Only for NULL values
questions.explanation: It changes the returned result only.

questions.question_text: What does UNION ALL preserve?
options: Only one copy per tuple
Only unmatched rows
Result multiplicity
Only nonnull values
questions.explanation: All branch rows remain.

questions.question_text: Can UNION remove repeats from within one branch?
options: No, only cross-branch copies
Only if a key is declared
Only for empty input
Yes
questions.explanation: Duplicate removal covers the combined output.

questions.question_text: Why can adding source_name preserve two previously merged rows?
options: It changes the compared tuple
It disables all comparisons
It changes every key
It forces a Cartesian join
questions.explanation: Different source labels make the selected tuples different.

questions.question_text: Do two NULL values always survive DISTINCT as separate set values?
options: Yes, always
No
Only if no ORDER BY exists
Only for integer columns
questions.explanation: Nulls are not distinct for duplicate elimination.

questions.question_text: Why can repeated workshop titles be legitimate?
options: Every repeated title is corruption
Titles are always primary keys
Different workshop identities may share a title
DISTINCT validates event identity
questions.explanation: A display label need not be unique.

questions.question_text: What can a case-insensitive collation affect?
options: The integer primary-key range
Whether tables can be joined
The number of selected columns
Whether differently cased text compares as duplicate
questions.explanation: Text comparison follows the applicable collation.

questions.question_text: Why is DISTINCT an unsafe blind fix for join repetition?
options: It can hide incorrect relationships or erase intended facts
It always makes queries slower
It always changes stored data
It prevents null comparisons
questions.explanation: First verify the intended grain and predicates.

questions.question_text: Which mechanism enforces an approved write-time uniqueness invariant?
options: SELECT DISTINCT alone
A suitable unique constraint or index
An ORDER BY clause
UNION ALL
questions.explanation: Read-time projection does not protect writes.

questions.question_text: What does COUNT after UNION ALL count?
options: Distinct people automatically
Only source tables
Retained combined observations
Only shared tuples
questions.explanation: The result population includes multiplicity.

questions.question_text: Which fixture exposes unsafe distinct amount summing?
options: Only one transaction
All different amounts
An empty table alone
Two separate transactions with equal amounts
questions.explanation: Equal measures can belong to different legitimate facts.

coding_problems.title: Combine distinct learner-course pairs
coding_problems.task: Return distinct learner_id,course_code pairs across both upload tables, ordered by learner_id,course_code.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE morning_uploads(learner_id INT,course_code INT NULL); CREATE TABLE afternoon_uploads(learner_id INT,course_code INT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO morning_uploads VALUES (1,10),(1,10),(2,NULL); INSERT INTO afternoon_uploads VALUES (1,10),(3,20),(2,NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT learner_id,course_code FROM morning_uploads UNION SELECT learner_id,course_code FROM afternoon_uploads ORDER BY learner_id,course_code;

constraints: Return distinct learner_id,course_code pairs across both upload tables, ordered by learner_id,course_code.

coding_problems.explanation: UNION compares full selected pairs, including null-valued course positions.

coding_problems.title: Count upload multiplicity across sources
coding_problems.task: Return learner_id,course_code,observations by pair across both sources, preserving repeated uploads before counting. Order by learner_id,course_code.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE morning_uploads(learner_id INT,course_code INT NULL); CREATE TABLE afternoon_uploads(learner_id INT,course_code INT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO morning_uploads VALUES (1,10),(1,10),(2,NULL); INSERT INTO afternoon_uploads VALUES (1,10),(3,20),(2,NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT learner_id,course_code,COUNT(*) AS observations FROM (SELECT learner_id,course_code FROM morning_uploads UNION ALL SELECT learner_id,course_code FROM afternoon_uploads) AS combined GROUP BY learner_id,course_code ORDER BY learner_id,course_code;
coding_problems.ordering: As specified by the task and explicit ORDER BY.
constraints: Return learner_id,course_code,observations by pair across both sources, preserving repeated uploads before counting. Order by learner_id,course_code.
edge_cases: The course dimension must not be dropped.
Repeated observations remain meaningful for this count.
hints: UNION ALL preserves observations and grouping counts their multiplicity.
coding_problems.explanation: UNION ALL preserves observations and grouping counts their multiplicity.

original_questions.question_text: What is the default duplicate-handling behavior of UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT?

All three remove duplicates by default (set semantics)
UNION keeps duplicates, but INTERSECT and EXCEPT remove them
Duplicate handling is undefined and varies randomly
original_questions.explanation: Every one of these three operations deduplicates by default.

original_questions.question_text: Which set operation has a universally-available 'ALL' variant to keep duplicates?
options: INTERSECT ALL
EXCEPT ALL
UNION ALL
None of them support an ALL variant
original_questions.explanation: UNION ALL is the widely-supported, commonly-used bag-semantics variant.

original_questions.question_text: Are INTERSECT ALL and EXCEPT ALL as widely supported as UNION ALL?
options: Yes, identically supported everywhere
No — they exist in some dialects (like PostgreSQL) but are far less commonly available or needed
No dialect supports INTERSECT ALL or EXCEPT ALL
They are more widely supported than UNION ALL
original_questions.explanation: UNION ALL is the dominant, most broadly available bag-semantics variant among the three operations.

original_questions.question_text: Do you ever need to explicitly opt OUT of deduplication to get the default deduplicating behavior?
options: Yes, deduplication must always be explicitly requested
No — deduplication IS the default; you explicitly opt INTO keeping duplicates instead (e.g. via ALL)
Deduplication cannot be controlled at all
This varies unpredictably by query
original_questions.explanation: The direction of the opt-in/opt-out is consistent: plain forms deduplicate, ALL variants keep duplicates.

original_questions.question_text: Why does duplicate handling matter for a downstream COUNT(*) on a combined result?
options: COUNT(*) is unaffected by whether duplicates were removed
Whether duplicates were removed directly changes how many rows COUNT(*) sees
COUNT(*) automatically ignores duplicates regardless of the set operation used
This only matters for INTERSECT, never UNION
original_questions.explanation: The actual row count of the combined result depends directly on whether deduplication happened.

original_questions.question_text: What practical question should precede choosing between a plain set operation and its ALL variant?
options: Whether the tables have the same name
Whether duplicates actually need to be removed for this specific use case
Whether ORDER BY will be used
Whether the query involves more than one table
original_questions.explanation: This is the core cost/correctness trade-off to consider before defaulting to the deduplicating form.

original_questions.question_text: Is deduplication free from a performance standpoint?
options: Yes, it costs nothing
No — comparing and removing duplicate rows requires real computational work
It only costs time for INTERSECT, not UNION or EXCEPT
Deduplication cost only applies to very large tables
original_questions.explanation: Deduplication always requires real comparison work, regardless of table size.

original_questions.question_text: If you know two data sources genuinely cannot overlap, is deduplication via plain UNION still useful?
options: Yes, it's always beneficial regardless
No — if overlap is impossible, UNION ALL produces the identical result faster, since there's nothing to deduplicate
Deduplication becomes mandatory in this case
This scenario cannot occur in practice
original_questions.explanation: When duplicates are provably impossible, UNION ALL gives the same correct result without paying the deduplication cost.
